newsitem.title: USA: Harcourt General wields power with cash bid.
newsitem.headline: Harcourt General wields power with cash bid.

text.p: Harcourt General Inc's surprise $740 million bid for National Education Corp is expected to entice nervous investors who have seen a swift erosion in the value of the target's month-old transaction with Sylvan Learning Systems Inc.

Although some Wall Street analysts said the National Education-Sylvan combination may provide a better strategic fit, they said that Sylvan's proposed stock transaction cannot compete with Harcourt General's cash offer.

"I think it's very good for the shareholders and the management of NEC. I would take Harcourt if I were the shareholders. In the longrun, Harcourt can really win it hands down," said Ivan Obolensky of investment firm Shields & Co.
Analysts also said that Harcourt, which is sitting on a cash stockpile of about $800 million, could raise its $19.50 offer if Sylvan tries to compete.

But they also said that Sylvan would be hardpressed to offer cash in the deal and would likely only sweeten the exchange ratio in its existing transaction - a move that could be dilutive and further erode its stock price.
Neither National Education nor Sylvan could be reached for comment on the Harcourt General offer.

The two companies last month announced a transaction in which National Education shareholders would receive 0.58 shares of Sylvan for each of their shares. But the stock deal, originally valued at $750 million, was worth just $625 million earlier this week due to a decline in Sylvan's share price.
Sylvan shares rose after Harcourt announced its bid, raising the value of its proposed transaction to $665 million - still less than Harcourt General's cash offer.

"While cash is cash, I still don't think this beats the Sylvan offer. I think NEC's strategy makes more sense with Sylvan," said Michael Moe of Montgomery Securities, noting that National Education's education and training business would benefit from being folded into Sylvan's distribution network.

But Harcourt defended its strategy, saying it is seeking to branch out from its role as a traditional textbook publisher into new areas, such as National Education's supplemental educational materials and correspondence courses.
"These are markets we have had an interest in. They fit very well into the company," said Harcourt spokesman Peter Farwell.
